newsitem.title: CANADA: Former Quebec premier fought for Canadian unity.
newsitem.headline: Former Quebec premier fought for Canadian unity.

text.p: Former Quebec Premier Robert Bourassa, who died on Wednesday at the age of 63, was an astute politician who managed to keep the French-speaking province within Canada.

Bourassa reigned over Quebec through its most troubled years, displaying a calm confidence that helped shield the fragile economy of this province of 7.3 million inhabitants from constant political uncertainty.

A staunch federalist but also a pragmatic nationalist, Bourassa worked to persuade Quebec residents and other Canadians to approve constitutional reforms that would have given Quebec more autonomy but kept it within the Canadian federation.

"Robert Bourassa is a walking paradox. The trajectory of his political life has paralleled Quebec's repeated attempts to assert its identity without jeopardising the armistice it made with English Canada," Quebec newspaper columnist Michel Vastel wrote in a 1991 book on Bourassa's political career.
Nicknamed "Boubou" by his friends, the lanky, Harvard-trained economist never inspired the love or pride Quebec voters felt toward ardent separatists like the current premier, Lucien Bouchard.
But Bourassa managed to win provincial elections in 1970, 1973, 1985 and 1989. In 1992 his support for the North American Free Trade Agreement helped sway Canadian opinion.
Bourassa spurred the development of Quebec's remote northern region through massive hydroelectric projects designed in part to export electricity to the northeastern United States.

Born in Montreal on July 14, 1933, Bourassa was the son of a government clerk. He graduated from the University of Montreal in 1956 and two years later married Quebec shipbuilding heiress Andree Simard.

Bourassa studied economics and political science at Oxford University for two years before receiving a master's degree from Harvard University in 1960. He was fiscal adviser to the Canadian government from 1960 to 1965 and an economics professor at Ottawa University from 1960 to 1963.

A master of ambiguity, Bourassa flirted with the fledgling separatist movement but rejected its hazy economic dreams. He was first elected as a Liberal Party deputy in the Quebec legislature on June 5, 1966.

Bourassa jumped into politics during the "Quiet Revolution," when Quebec's French Canadians emerged from more than 200 years of English Canadian control of the province's economy and from domination by the Roman Catholic Church. He was elected leader of the Quebec Liberal Party on Jan. 17, 1970, and four months later, at the age of 36, he became Quebec's youngest-ever premier.

Within four months, he was confronted with the "October Crisis," when the left-wing nationalist Front de Liberation du Quebec (Quebec Liberation Front) kidnapped Quebec Labour Minister Pierre Laporte and British Trade Commissioner James Cross in Montreal. Cross was freed, but Laporte was found, strangled, in the trunk of a car.
In response to the crisis, Canadian Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau stationed troops in Montreal and suspended civil rights, permitting the arrest and detention of several hundred political activists.

Bourassa emerged from the crisis looking like a feeble and inexperienced leader, but he was re-elected premier in 1973. As Quebec nationalists' brief flirtation with violence ended, Bourassa was swept from office in the 1976 provincial election by the separatist Parti Quebecois led by a highly popular former journalist, Rene Levesque.

Branded by some in the Quebec media as the "most hated man" in Quebec politics, Bourassa went into self-imposed exile in Brussels, Paris and Boston, studying and teaching economics. He returned to Quebec to take an active role in the 1980 referendum campaign on the separation of Quebec from Canada. The separatists received only 40 percent of the vote.

In 1983, Bourassa was re-elected leader of the Quebec Liberal Party and staged a remarkable comeback by winning the December 1985 provincial election, recapturing the faith of Quebeckers weary of the separatist option.
In 1987 he joined then Canadian Prime Minister Brian Mulroney in the first of two failed attempts to reform the Canadian constitution, adopted from England in 1982 without Quebec's consent.
